#6950. John Madden Deserved Better Than a Messy Amazon Biopic

A movie can have all the makings of a winner and still fumble the ball.

As a movie critic, I’m not in the business of telling professional filmmakers what they could or should do with their art. What an unproductive way to do my job. But sometimes I see something so egregious, and so boneheaded, I’m compelled to scream from my seat, forehead running hot and veins bulging out—like a coach forced to watch his wide receiver telegraph his route to the defense like a GPS in cleats. That’s how I felt watching MADDEN.

Streaming now on Prime Video, right on time for Thanksgiving football, is David O. Russell’s MADDEN. It’s a big streaming snooze where Nicolas Cage dons a fat suit and putzes around in a confused performance that flip-flops on which part of the legendary coach-turned-broadcaster-turned-foot-spray-spokesman’s interiority we’re meant to sympathize with. The real John Madden suffered cognitive decline until his death in 2021, but Cage’s performance is another exhausting exercise of actors playing undiagnosed dementia—and MADDEN has no calcium in its bones to even commit to that.

Devoid of suspense, stakes, or really any answer to the question “Why?” MADDEN is a plotless dud that falls short in its game plan of probing the unbearable weight of a massive legacy. Worst of all, the spine of a fantastic movie is all there. It’s just not in playing shape. To wit: Scrubbed from the trailers is the reason anyone under the age of 35 knows John Madden’s name: video games. (It is my personal conspiracy theory this was done to mitigate losing an audience of boomer granddads, who will fire up the movie on their Roku before passing out on tryptophan.) In 1988, the former Raiders coach who scribbled on screens lent his name to a project by a small tech company called Electronic Arts. Today it’s valued at $55 billion and owned by Saudis. But back then it was just a start-up full of nerds making a football-simulation video game called Madden NFL, which has since morphed into an industry juggernaut that rakes in the equivalent of a small country’s gross domestic product.

The men and women of Madden’s era are obviously unable to fathom computer games as a big deal. (Even now, on the eve of Grand Theft Auto VI, I have heard from people grossly underestimating its economic and cultural power.) In the film is John Mulaney as Trip Hawkins, the founder of EA, whose wiry physique, skinny ties, and plaid button-downs stand in contrast to the movie’s many beefcake extras who exude ’70s-flavored machismo. But Trip’s presence in the film exists to warn the chain-smoking dinosaurs of their coming extinction. Cementing a legacy is not about winning so much that they make a bronze bust and stick you in the Hall of Fame, with the other dead guys. It’s about making your name mean something. No one sees the future until it’s in front of them—you can only hope you can find your way to be part of it somehow. And somehow John Madden did just that. Unfortunately, even MADDEN fails to recognize the awesome potential of its own story.

Russell’s latest work spends the first half cosplaying as a sober sports biopic, in the vein of Moneyball, until it eventually and perhaps inevitably pivots into a low-stakes tech-business success story like BlackBerry or AIR. This alone isn’t a bad thing—frankly, it should be the entire movie—but MADDEN’s failure to synthesize its core themes about how men can actually live forever is what makes the movie such a frustrating experience to sit through.

MADDEN (the movie, all caps) is concerned with legacy. What does it mean? What does it really take to be remembered? For Cage’s Madden, it starts out as a straightforward idea: win Super Bowls. Football runs in his blood and runs his house; early on, Kathryn Hahn, as Madden’s wife, Virginia, scolds her son for rooting for the wrong team. Raiders football is what feeds and clothes them, she says. Thanking Raiders football is akin to thanking God. When the Raiders start winning and a retired Madden watches quite pathetically with a microphone in his hand, you can see the thousand-yard stare in his eyes as he considers abandoning his faith. Later, Christian Bale’s gel-slicked Al Davis, the owner of the Raiders whose rings form a set of brass knuckles, tries to convince Madden to come back—because winning is all it takes to be remembered, and winning is all that matters.

Before this movie, I had never heard of Al Davis, but I have played plenty of Madden on PlayStation. By the end of the movie (minor spoilers), Cage spends Thanksgiving with his preteen granddaughter, who whomps his butt with a controller in her hands. You can see what MADDEN is getting at here. Real legacy cannot be measured in rings or bronze statues but in the joy you inspire in others. Like it or not, a best-selling video game is how today’s generation of professional athletes stayed interested in the sport, and it might be John Madden’s single greatest contribution to football, more than anything he’s ever done on the field.

Unfortunately, Russell’s slipshod direction ensures that nothing in the movie clicks and nothing in it breathes. Trite dialogue and a flat visual palette that’s barely a notch above Hallmark movies keep it on the bench. As it stands, MADDEN is simply not the movie I would have made. But I’m just screaming from the nosebleeds.

#6949. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’s Cast Is Totally Stacked

See Joseph Zada, Whitney Peak, Elle Fanning, Kieran Culkin, Jesse Plemons, and Glenn Close in the new movie

The Hunger Games franchise is welcoming a new installment, Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film adaptation of Suzanne Collins’s best-selling dystopian saga.

Releasing on November 20, the film boasts a star-studded cast of about 33 actors and counting, poised to bring a blend of familiar names and new faces to the world of Panem.

Ahead of the film, we’re reacquainting ourselves with beloved characters from the original trilogy, like Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning), Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin), Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.), and Wiress (Maya Hawke). Even the completely new characters, like Maysilee Donner and Lenore Dove, have family ties to well-known characters in the franchise.

Based on Collins’s second prequel novel, Sunrise on the Reaping delves into the brutal 50th Hunger Games, spotlighting a young Haymitch Abernathy 24 years before he became Katniss and Peeta’s mentor. We, as readers, thought we knew a detailed account of the second Quarter Quell from Mockingjay, but as we learn in the Sunrise on the Reaping novel, much of what we learned was manipulated by the Capitol to be used as propaganda.

This much is still true: With twice the tributes, the 50th Hunger Games doubles the bloodshed, trauma, and size of the cast. To prepare for the inevitably heart-wrenching film, get to know the extensive cast.

Joseph Zada is a 21-year-old Australian actor best known for playing Johnny Sinclair in the television series We Were Liars and Cal Trask in East of Eden.

Zada shows a very different side of Woody Harrelson’s character, before the biting sarcasm and heavy drinking. In the new film, we follow 16-year-old Haymitch’s harrowing journey through the 50th Hunger Games and, arguably, a more distressing journey after victory. We knew Zada was perfect for the role when he discussed re-creating Harrelson’s Mockingjay Part 2 red-carpet pajama moment.

Elle Fanning is a 28-year-old American actress best known for her roles as Aurora in Maleficent, Syvie Russo in A Complete Unknown, and Catherine in The Great, as well as being half of an iconic sister duo with Dakota Fanning.

While Trinket is only a side character in Sunrise on the Reaping, her casting was one of the most highly anticipated, with fans almost unanimously agreeing that Fanning was the only correct choice to reprise Elizabeth Banks’s character. In Sunrise on the Reaping, Trinket is a young member of the Capitol styling and beauty team for District 12.

It’s possible that Suzanne Collins got tired of the endless Coriolanus Snow thirst edits on TikTok and went ahead and cast Voldemort. No, really, 63-year-old English actor Ralph Fiennes is best known for his role as Voldemort in the Harry Potter film series.

Fiennes plays President Snow, a younger version of the late Donald Sutherland’s character in the original trilogy and an older version of Tom Blythe’s character in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. President Snow reaches his peak level of viciousness in Sunrise on the Reaping, and Fiennes is the perfect vessel to carry out Snow’s evil plans.

Kieran Culkin is a 44-year-old actor best known for his roles in A Real Pain and Succession. Despite recently winning an Oscar, Emmy, Golden Globe, and SAG Award, his brother Macaulay still has him beat in household name recognition for his childhood role in Home Alone. Reprising Stanley Tucci's role as Hunger Games host Caesar Flickerman may change that.

Jesse Plemons is a 38-year-old actor best known for his roles in Friday Night Lights and Breaking Bad (and for being married to Kirsten Dunst). In another impeccable casting choice, Plemons also played the son of the original Plutarch (the late Philip Seymour Hoffman) in The Master (2012).

In both Sunrise on the Reaping and the original trilogy, Plutarch Heavensbee is an old-money Capitol citizen whose morally gray philosophies make him one of the franchise’s most fascinating characters. In the new film, we see him as a young, ambitious cameraman, years before he became head gamemaker.

Lili Taylor is a 59-year-old American actress and author best known for her roles in Mystic Pizza and The Conjuring. She has the perfect sweet smile to play Mags Flanagan, the victor of the 11th Hunger Games from District 4.

Mags, previously played by the late Lynn Cohen, was introduced in Catching Fire when she volunteered to take Annie Cresta's place in the 75th Hunger Games. In Sunrise on the Reaping, Mags acts as District 12's mentor, as they have no surviving winners of their own.

Maya Hawke is the 28-year-old daughter of Uma Thurman and Ethan Hawke, best known for her roles as Robin in Stranger Things and Anxiety in Inside Out 2.

She plays Wiress, the District 3 victor fresh out of the 49th Hunger Games. Amanda Plummer played the character in Catching Fire, when she was reaped with Beetee as the 75th Hunger Games District 3 tributes.

Kelvin Harrison Jr. is a 32-year-old actor who previously played the son of the original Beetee (Jeffrey Wright) in Monsters (2018).

As the Hunger Games fan account Panem Propaganda said, “If I had a nickel for every time a Sunrise on the Reaping cast member played the son of their older Hunger Games counterpart in a completely unrelated movie, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice,” referring to the castings of Beetee and Plutarch.

Beetee was the winner of the 34th Hunger Games from District 3 who was reaped for the 75th Hunger Games in Catching Fire. The new film delves into his heartbreaking backstory, involving the fate of his son, Ampert, as well as his secret plan with Haymitch to disrupt the games.

Iris Apatow is a 24-year-old actress who previously appeared in This Is 40, The Bubble, and Knocked Up. She is the daughter of actress Leslie Mann and producer Judd Apatow, the sister of Euphoria star Maude Apatow, and the girlfriend of White Lotus star Sam Nivola. She plays Proserpina Trinket, Effie’s younger sister and member of the District 12 prep team.

Edvin Ryding is a 23-year-old Swedish actor who previously appeared in 28 Years Later and Young Royals. He plays Vitus, Proserpina’s friend and sidekick on the District 12 prep team.

Whitney Peak is a 23-year-old Ugandan-Canadian actress best known for her role as Zoya in the 2021 Gossip Girl reboot. She plays Lenore Dove, the Covey singer and love of Haymitch's life.

Though her character is unique to Sunrise on the Reaping, Lenore Dove is rumored to be the daughter of either Maude Ivory or Lucy Gray Baird. Fans can’t help but notice the resemblance between Peak and Rachel Zegler.

McKenna Grace is a 20-year-old actress best known for her roles in The Handmaid's Tale, Ghostbusters: Afterlife, and Young Sheldon. While young, she has been acting since she was five, and she has had at least 34 film and television roles.

She plays Maysilee Donner, the spoiled mean girl who turns into a star when she is reaped for the 50th Hunger Games. She has a twin sister, Merrilee (whose daughter later gifts Katniss the Mockingjay pin), and is friends with Asterid March, Katniss's mother. She allies herself with Haymitch during the game, and the two share a sibling-like bond.

Ben Wang is a 29-year-old actor best known for his roles in Karate Kid: Legends and American Born Chinese.

He plays Wyatt Callow, Haymitch's fellow District 12 boy tribute. The Callow family runs the gambling scene in District 12, placing bets on the Hunger Games tributes each year.

Wang’s Instagram is @definitelynotbenwang.

Glenn Close is a 79-year-old Tony, Emmy, and Golden Globe winner best known for her roles in Fatal Attraction, 101 Dalmatians, and The Deliverance.

She plays Drusilla Sickle, the District 12 tributes’ escort. Drusilla is known for her many cosmetic surgeries that poorly attempt to disguise her age. She and Maysilee are the biggest divas in Panem, and their personalities clash disastrously.

Billy Porter is a 57-year-old Emmy, Tony, and Grammy Award–winning actor, singer, composer, director, and playwright.

He plays Magno Stift, the incompetent stylist for the District 12 tributes. His personal style involves wearing a plethora of live reptiles, and his hobbies include licking frogs for the psychedelic effects.

Molly McCann is a young Irish actress who previously appeared in Bad Sisters, Herself, and Rosie. She plays Louella McCoy, a young girl from District 12 who Haymitch views as a little sister and nicknamed “Sweetheart.” Fans were quick to notice McCann's resemblance to Katniss (Jennifer Laurence), the only other character who Haymitch refers to as Sweetheart.

McCann’s Instagram is @mollymccannactress.

Iona Bell is a young English actress who plays Louella’s uncanny lookalike, Lou Lou.

Her Instagram is @iona_bell_official_actor.

Kara Tointon is a 43-year-old English actress who previously appeared in EastEnders, The Teacher, and Too Good to Be True. She plays Willamae Abernathy, Haymitch's mother.

#6941. Movado’s New Tempo-Matic Watch Is Inspired by an Iconic Piece from the ’70s

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Proof once again that it’s hip to be square.

Movado was founded in 1881 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, which isn’t a particularly odd backstory for a heritage Swiss watch brand. But it has been American owned since 1983 and has a distinct quality tied deeply to its long history in the U.S. market—which puts it slightly outside the predictable purview of many watch collectors.

Right now, a growing band of horological nerds is finding rich pickings in the Movado back catalog and pushing up vintage prices considerably—especially for its mid-century chronographs and its legendary Museum Watch (which celebrates 80 years in 2027; more of that to come) in the process.

It’s not only the collectors who are digging into Movado’s past, however. Last month, the brand released the Heritage Tempo-Matic ($995–$1,095), a re-creation of a watch that merges sporty and retro design in a neat and slinky package. The Tempo-Matic, Movado’s first automatic movement, was launched in 1945 and went on to power a broad range of Movado’s wristwatches. But the rounded yet boxy “TV” shape of the new Heritage Tempo-Matic is unmistakably 1970s, when watch design took a giant leap forward into sexy new territory.

The 2026 version is available in three executions, each powered by the reliable Sellita SW200-1B movement and fitted with integrated steel bracelets that positively scream seventies. Two of them come in brushed steel with vertically brushed burgundy or blue dials. A third—which, we must admit, is our favorite—is gold-tone PVD with a warm gray dial. You’d be hard-pressed to find such an elegant, authentic, and affordable homage to the 1970s—a decade that’s currently a very hot motif in watch-collecting circles—anywhere else.

For further Movado inspiration, you might enjoy a glimpse into the brand’s rich watchmaking history at the Horological Society of New York, a fascinating nonprofit organization—effectively a guild created to support immigrant German watchmakers—that since 1866 has promoted the art and science of watchmaking in America. In the guild’s expansive watchmaking library, until July 2027, a dedicated display charts the Movado brand’s achievements in watchmaking, advertising, and design from as early as the ahead-of-its-time, art-deco-style Polyplan of 1912. Visits to the Movado exhibit are free, but we advise you to call ahead to check availability. And if you really get the bug while you’re there, you might like to sign up for membership, regular lectures, and even a series of watchmaking workshops where you get hands-on watchmaking experience under expert tutorship.

#6939. Who Is Daddy Franklin From ‘The Body’? For Starters, Nnamdi Asomugha Is Kerry Washington’s Husband

Daddy Franklin is married to Olivia Pope?

If you watched The Body in one sitting and are now fully obsessed with it, you’re not alone!! The horrifying coming-of-age series is scary good, and while you may not be familiar with the actor who plays Father Samuel Franklin (aka Daddy Franklin), you definitely know his very famous wife. As it turns out, Nnamdi Asomugha has been married to Kerry Washington for over 13 years now, having fallen in love after watching Kerry perform in Race on Broadway in 2010. Kerry later confirmed the story during a 2018 interview with Marie Claire, saying, “The last time I did theater, it completely transformed my life. That’s where I met my husband.” Cute!!!

Though things got off to a rocky start (Kerry apparently told Nnamdi she didn’t date athletes, and Nnamdi told Kerry he didn’t date actors), the two got together anyway, and just about three years later in June 2013, they tied the knot in a super low-key ceremony. According to their marriage license, Kerry and Nnamdi said “I do” in Hailey, Idaho, where Nnamdi’s sister officiated and Kerry’s parents served as witnesses. Since then, the couple has welcomed two kids together—Isabelle Amarachi, born in 2014, and Caleb Kelechi, born in 2016—and are seemingly thriving outside of the spotlight. But we think it’s time to learn a lil bit more about Nnamdi, don’t you?

Here’s everything you should know about the man behind Daddy Franklin, including how he rose to fame as a former NFL cornerback and what he’s up to next.

After growing up in Louisiana in a Nigerian Igbo household, Nnamdi attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he played for the California Golden Bears football team. Soon after graduating, Nnamdi was drafted in the first round of the 2003 NFL Draft by the Oakland Raiders, which is very impressive.

Over his 11-year professional football career, Nnamdi also played for the Philadelphia Eagles and the San Francisco 49ers, and in December 2013, the cornerback signed a one-day contract with Oakland so he could retire as a Raider. I love to see a loyal man!

According to Nnamdi, the decision to retire at 32 was difficult, but it still felt like the right time for him. “Yeah, I felt that it was a good time, but it didn’t make it any easier,” he told UPROXX. “It’s a game that 'til this day I miss, and I miss playing. It’s not that I want to go play again, but I miss so many aspects of it; being around the team, being around the coaching, that calm before the storm.”

Nnamdi first caught the acting bug all the way back in 2008, when he landed the role of “Party Guest with Wife” on the CW sitcom The Game. (Remember: There are no small roles, only small actors!!) He then caught the eye of director Peter Berg on the set of a Nike commercial shoot in 2009, who was impressed by the athlete’s ease in front of the camera. From there, Nnamdi went on to play small roles in Friday Night Lights, Leverage, and Cubed before making his on-screen feature film debut in 2012’s Fire with Fire.

Since retiring from the NFL, Nnamdi has fully committed himself to his acting career with starring roles in the films Crown Heights, Sylvie’s Love, The Good Nurse, The Knife, and—most recently—The Body. He’s also served as a producer on several of those projects as well.

Despite all his success, Nnamdi still remains as modest as ever, avoiding social media and press to instead focus on his craft. “I’m really bad at self-promotion. I know that about myself,” he previously explained to Bleacher Report back in 2017. “People told me all of the time, ‘You could be such a big star if you just talked about yourself more,’ but I’m not good at that. It’s always been about team.”

During a 2018 interview with Today, Kerry corrected a host when they alluded to her two children, saying, “I’m a mother of three." The reason: Nnamdi has a now-teenage daughter from another relationship, who Kerry has helped raise alongside her two biological children. And just like with Isabelle and Caleb, the couple keeps their eldest far from the paparazzi, so very little is known about her.

As Kerry joked to People, “I have moments where I take pictures or videos of one of my three amazing kids and I wanna post it online, and I tend to just send it to my parents or my shrink instead.”

Philanthropy is important to Nnamdi, which is why he created the Asomugha Foundation in 2005 at the very beginning of his career.

The foundation has two main programs: Orphans and Widows in Need (which provides food, shelter, medicine, vocational training, literacy efforts, and scholarships to widows and orphans in Nigeria) and Asomugha College Tour for Scholars (which takes selected students from Bay Area and Los Angeles area high schools on college tours across the country).

Though Kerry and Nnamdi are both actors and producers, it isn’t often that they work together on creative projects. Back in 2017, Nnamdi told Vanity Fair that it was possible he and his wife would co-produce a project at some point.

“We would produce,” he said. “We’d probably produce before acting, I would think.” The following year, his production company, iAm21 Entertainment, helped produce American Son, a Broadway play starring Kerry, and hopefully, that won’t be the last time the two are involved in the same project.

As far as sharing the screen goes, however, Nnamdi doesn’t think that will ever happen. As he told The New York Times, “I produced American Son, but as actors, there’s no plan as of now for that collaboration. We’re very supportive of each other’s journeys, but we’ve always been that way. We always want the best for each other in whatever we’re doing.”

Case in point? The couple’s *chef’s kiss* appearance at the 2025 Met Gala. Ahem:

Oh, and the duo’s 2025 Golden Globes looks:

And ofc, he was right by Kerry's side during her December 2024 Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony, where she finally received her well-deserved star. How cute do they look with Kerry's parents??

TL;DR: Kerry and Nnamdi truly couldn’t be any cuter. Keep on being adorably low-key, you two.

#6937. Plestia Alaqad Sees the World

The photojournalist talks about the making of her latest book, The Eyes of Gaza

“The hardest part was having something as intimate and personal as a diary become public,” says Plestia Alaqad of her decision to publish her diary-memoir, The Eyes of Gaza. The book details the harrowing first weeks after October 7 in Gaza as a young Palestinian journalist. Alaqad studied new media and journalism at Eastern Mediterranean University in Cyprus before returning to her home in 2022. Intending to educate the world about her city, she did not know she would end up reporting the first stages of the genocide.

Alaqad’s reporting situated herself as a voice for the ordinary. In the first few days, she spoke to her neighbors and local children. Her reporting appeared mostly on her Instagram account, which grew to a little over 2 million followers, with many of her images republished by the BBC, The New York Times, PBS NewsHour, and The Washington Post. Even through the chaos and the expulsion of over 100,000 Gazans in the first few days, according to UNHCR, which Alaqad also recounts in her memoir, there are moments of tenderness caught by her and everyday Gazans she would meet and talk to. Her style of reporting is grounded in a sense of familiarity, narrating the everyday in extraordinary circumstances. She made connections with people in a way that makes you feel like you were alongside her, drinking tea with the local tetas and jiddos, watching the violence and the world collapse around you.

Alaqad left Gaza for Lebanon, where she is completing her master’s degree. During the course of our interview, she spoke openly with me about the loneliness of the isolation of being a witness, forever changed by the devastation.

One of my favorite things about Gaza is the people and the sense of community. For example, the relationship between my neighbors and I. I’ve been living in the Al -Waleed Building since I was almost four years old, and I know all my neighbors. Like Dana, who lived next door next to me—it was like having a sister and best friend nearby at all times. Whenever I needed anything, I just knocked at Dana’s door. If I needed help picking out an outfit, if I needed help replying to messages, even if I was just bored and I wanted someone to hang out with, it was always Dana who I turned to. There’s something about Gaza that just is home to me. There is simplicity and a love for life in Gaza that I haven’t seen elsewhere in the world. So being born and raised there always meant having loving and supportive people around me.

There’s more to us than being occupied. We’re full of talent and art we never got the time to make, because we’re too busy worrying if the people we love will still be alive tomorrow. That’s what pushes me to keep writing.

I’m interested in writing and telling stories of people. I recently interviewed Renad Atallah and wrote a piece about her for The New Arab. Also, one of my favorite pieces I wrote was an interview with Alaa Abu Diab, a one-of-a-kind comedian, for The National.

As of recently, I started my newsletter on Substack, where I share a personal essay every week on Gaza, girlhood, friendship, and everything in between. My ultimate hope would be to tell stories about a free Palestine one day. And as a journalist, I’ll always see my work as incomplete without going back to Gaza and continuing to tell Palestinian stories from the ground. And hopefully work on an international level and tell stories of people who suffered because of war and conflicts in other countries.

I enjoy reading nonfiction books and memoirs because I love learning about people and their experiences. I remember reading Anne Frank’s diary in middle school.… I remember how it made me feel and the impact it had on me.

I have also always been drawn to personal writings, like Franz Kafka’s letters and the letters between Ghassan Kanafani and Ghada al-Samman. I think I’m a very curious person by nature, and I’m interested in understanding what is happening in people’s minds, and if I get the chance to read strangers’ diaries, I wouldn't say no. That curiosity is something that inspired me.

Growing up, I always had a diary. It was me and my purple diary against the world.… For me, journaling has always been my safe space in the world. It’s the one place where I can write whatever I want without feeling judged. That’s honestly why I wanted to create Neya [Alaqad’s creative brand], which is an Arabic word that means intention. The first product will be a journal, of course, and it will come in four different colors. Each journal has a small, kind reminder on the hardcover and little sweet quotes throughout the pages because I wanted to create something that is personal and safe, something you would want to come back to and share your thoughts in. For me, journaling has always been where I can reconnect with myself. I hope Neya can become that for other people too: a small space where they can pause, reflect, and reconnect with themselves.

The hardest part was having something as intimate and personal as a diary become public. Something that was once only mine suddenly was in the hands of people from all around the world. I always try to think about the impact it could have on others, and I’m grateful that this time we get to tell our own stories rather than having our stories told on our behalf. I’m also grateful for the readers around the world who have read The Eyes of Gaza and are making the effort to educate themselves about Palestine.

I often feel like I am living in two worlds. On one hand, I have the opportunity to do things that many people back home cannot access freely, such as pursuing my education and continuing my master’s degree. On the other hand, I carry the weight of knowing what is happening to my people and my land, without having any superpower to stop it.

I always try to stay honest and true to myself, and I try to take people through this journey with me online. I share the contradictions, the pain, and the moments of hope. What it’s like trying to process the experience of having your homeland bombed, your city erased, and your people murdered, while also surviving and trying to make sense of the world outside. It is something that is difficult to put into words.

It feels like time has frozen in Gaza, while the rest of the world continues moving forward. And for those of us away from home, we are constantly trying to live between these two realities.

Gaza is a place where contradictions exist side by side. You see unimaginable grief, but you also see people trying to find meaning and strength in the middle of that suffering.

The Eyes of Gaza captures these contradictions. On one page, sadness may take over, while on another, hope emerges. Ultimately, I believe that when people experience powerful emotions, they are often moved to take action.

#6936. The MacBook Neo Is on Sale for the First Time Ever

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Grab this early Black Friday deal before it sells out.

I am not the first person to point out that MacBooks are expensive. I will not be the last. If you monitor this stuff like we do, you’ll have seen the irony that Apple released the budget-conscious MacBook Neo earlier this year—only for the global computing shortage to almost immediately raise the price from $599 to $699.

But the Neo is still cheap. You could buy it for full price and get your money’s worth—although scoring it on sale makes the whole thing even sweeter. Just in time for Black Friday, Amazon shaved $50 off of the buzzy MacBook. Chalk it up to a Christmas miracle.

Designed as Apple’s answer to the lower-budget laptops running Windows, the Neo’s target audience is technically students—hence the good branding and cool colors. That being said, if you need a personal computer for watching Netflix and doing your taxes but don’t want a full desktop, it’s a perfect choice.

The Neo runs on Apple’s A18 Pro chip—the same one that powers the iPhone 16 Pro and Pro Max. If the idea of buying a laptop that runs on a phone chip gives you pause, your stress is better channeled elsewhere. While this isn’t the right device for someone who is planning to run heavy-duty software, it can handle standard Internet browsing, video calls, and the like with ease. Just keep in mind that it has only 8 GB of RAM, so it’s best suited to basic workflows.

Of course, this computer has the added benefit of four jazzy color options: blush and citrus for the bold, indigo for those more subdued, and silver for that classic MacBook aesthetic. Wrapped in an aluminum body with a 13-inch Liquid Retina display, the Neo weighs in at just 2.7 pounds (same as the MacBook Air) and is 0.5 inches thick. (For reference, the iPhone 17 Pro Max is 0.35 inches thick.)

Despite our best efforts, we don’t quite know how Apple determines its deals for big sale events, so there’s no telling if this $50 discount is as good as it’s going to get for Black Friday. In all honesty, we were hoping Amazon would shave $100 off to get the Neo back to its pre-increase price. In our wildest dreams, we’re gunning for a deal that would make this the first-ever sub-$500 MacBook.

We’re not giving up on a deeper discount once Black Friday proper arrives, but for now the Neo is undoubtedly a smart buy for anyone who wants a laptop that can handle all of the basics. At $649, it’s still a fraction of the cost of the MacBook Air and Pro.

#6933. Prince Harry Says Moving to England Has Given Archie and Lili a Big Confidence Boost

The royal sat down for his first TV appearance since returning to England

Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are all settled into their new life in England, it seems—but it wasn’t a simple transition. Today, Prince Harry sat down for a rare chat on U.K. daytime show This Morning—his first television appearance since returning to England—and opened up about the changes his kids have gone through since the move in late August.

Harry said of his children: “They love being back! I say back, they never really...”

“It’s a big culture shift ... The kids in school uniforms is a big change for them, but it’s certainly helped,” he added. “The confidence in both of them has gone through the roof since being at a U.K. school, which is really, really nice.”

Harry also touched on his kids’ accents, which seem to be leaning British these days. The prince joked that he is “squeezing the accents,” and Archie and Lili’s “friends at school are doing the same.” He noted that “Lili does a good impression of ‘Mummy.’”

Harry’s TV appearance came a couple days after he and wife Duchess Meghan were seen out with their kids for the first time since their move (though the couple has made some public outings without the children). The family went to Winter Wonderland, an annual six-week Christmas festival and fair in London’s Hyde Park.

Elsewhere during his TV chat, the Duke of Sussex discussed the upcoming Invictus Games, which are set to take place in July 2027 in Birmingham, England. Harry has been participating in related events leading up to the games, and over the weekend even made an appearance at the Invictus Games in Lviv, Ukraine.

#6925. This Unexpected French Antique Is Suddenly Making a Comeback, and You’ve Probably Seen It Before

The desire to preserve mementos from a wedding day transcends centuries and cultures. Today's brides still hang onto their wedding dresses, dry their bouquets, and spend a large portion of their budgets on photography. But in 19th- and 20th-century France, the art of preserving wedding-day memories took the form of globes de mariée, also known as marriage globes.

These ornate, shrine-like displays primarily showcased the bride's head crown and other keepsakes from the big day, and the additional pieces inside symbolized the couple's dreams for their life together. The cloche protected these special items from dust back then and still today.

Here's a closer look at the history and allure of globes de mariée, plus tips for sourcing and styling these gorgeous antiques.

Chris Featherston is the senior vice president of product acquisition at Austin Auction Gallery, and he and his family have been dealing in French antiques for more than 30 years. In the last couple of years alone, they've sold more than 150 globes de Mariée for an average of $400 to $600 each.

But this definitely wasn't always the case. Featherstone notes that the demand for these antiques has risen significantly in the past five years alone.

"In the early days of our business, most of what we sold came from house clearances in France," he recalls. "These globes were ubiquitous. At that time, we felt lucky to be able to sell them for $30 to $40 each."

Anyone with a strong appreciation for historic relics can see the appeal of these antiques. For instance, Mick and Paige Whitcomb have been collecting globes de mariée for nearly a decade, and they currently own 15. Their interest in these types of treasures is reflected in their careers. Mick creates sculptural lighting from architectural and industrial salvage dating back to the 1800s through his business, Artifacts by Nomad. Paige is a tintype photographer who captures staged scenes featuring antiques from the 1800s (including her globes de mariée) using a 19th-century large-format studio camera.

"While traveling in France for a wedding anniversary, we were first exposed to globes de mariée at the Marché aux Puces antique market in Paris," Mick says. "While we were initially caught by the beauty of the objects, after hearing their history and connection to French marriages, it felt like a beautiful way of commemorating our anniversary and trip to Europe."

Due to the highly custom nature of globes de marriée, each one is a unique find. However, Featherston notes that most contain a few similar components. For starters, the bride's headpiece often rests on a red cushion, and it typically shows off delicate beeswax orange blossoms that symbolize purity and virginity.

Most also contain small mirrors, which carried different meanings depending on the shape. For example, diamond-shaped mirrors symbolize how many children the couple wished to have, and rectangular mirrors stood for the length of time the couple knew each other before their engagement.

You'll also often find a wreath embellished with brass ornaments, usually flowers, birds and tree leaves. These symbolize love, a long-lasting marriage, and happiness.

"The globes de marriées integrate beautiful symbolism in every piece, and I find them fascinating," Paige says. "Each globe is so distinctive, and tells the story of the couple that created it. You can surmise the couple's hopes and dreams by minutiae tucked away behind the dome for safekeeping. I find very intimate details incorporated into the displays, such as a prayer card of a favorite saint, to photos of the bride and groom. I have even found hair and teeth, transforming the antique into a memento mori as well."

Mick has noticed that sourcing these antiques is considerably more difficult in the United States than in Europe. But with a little patience and determination, it is possible.

"Because of the glass domes, I think fewer importers are brave enough to bring them over," he says. "Despite this, we have found the occasional gem in the wild." In the States, he's had the most luck sourcing them from design-forward antique dealers, online auction sites and even prop houses that have just wrapped up a period film project.

Since there is a constant demand for these pieces, Featherston tries to feature several in every sale at Austin Auction Gallery.

Globes de mariée can add a formal and traditional flair to any space, and they even mix well with more modern accents.

"One of my favorite ways to showcase the globes de mariée is to mix them with a piece of contemporary art," Paige says. "I love to create a harmony between our collections of antiques and artwork from artists that are living and working today."

For example, Mick and Paige have styled two of their favorite globes de mariée with the piece "The Gardener" by working artist L.J. Eidolon. "I find collecting modern works that have a historic feeling to them helps create balance between the multiple centuries displayed together in one scene," Paige says.

#6922. Lafayette 148’s Emily Smith on 30 Years in Fashion and Finding Her Uniform

In ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Lafayette 148 creative director Emily Smith as the New York-based fashion house celebrates its 30th anniversary. Smith has spent more than two decades at the helm of the brand, working her way up from a part-time freelancer to creative lead. But her fashion ambitions began long before she arrived in New York. Growing up in Atlanta, she ran her own neighborhood art camp before discovering designers like Donna Karan and realizing fashion could be a career. Now, Smith is celebrating the women who have shaped Lafayette 148 through its “Uniform” campaign, which highlights accomplished New Yorkers and their individual approaches to personal style. Below, Smith reflects on her unconventional start, why she’s stayed at the company for over 20 years, and the career advice she wishes she’d followed sooner.

I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher. It was basically babysitting all the neighborhood kids, but I created a flyer, got paid for it, and did the whole thing. I started in second grade, and we did it every year for about eight years. I even started hiring people so we could have two classes going at once. We had swimming lessons. The local news even came and did a segment on it. I loved decorating my classroom and setting everything up. My parents were so nice to give me the garage and basement to do it all. Not necessarily an official job, but my first money-making moment.

I was a bagger at Kroger. It just was not for me.

I was always creative growing up. At a certain point, I discovered Donna Karan. It’s kind of crazy when you see somebody doing something and suddenly realize, Oh, that’s a career. I can do that. I became obsessed with everything in the ’90s, all the New York fashion at the time. That was when I decided I wanted to pursue it. When college applications came around, my mom really encouraged me to go to art school. I started in fashion, and that became my focus. Growing up in Atlanta, I wasn’t necessarily surrounded by a big fashion community. But my dad’s office was across the street from the art museum at one point, and I remember going there and having that exposure. My mom was always crafty and creative, too. She really encouraged us to be who we were.

There’s a language creative people have that’s a little different from the way business people communicate. When I went to art school, I felt like I’d found my people. It wasn’t just fashion people. It was photographers, fine artists, and all these different kinds of creatives. Being around people who thought about things differently was really inspiring. Even today, I thrive around people who have creative insight. There’s always a little more depth to the way they see things.

I interned at Bill Blass for about six months. I moved to New York in July 2001, and we had our fashion show on September 10. I remember Marc Jacobs had his show that day, too, and everybody was celebrating. People were saying, “Just come a little late to work tomorrow.” And then, obviously, September 11 happened. A week later, the entire team was let go, from the top down. What I learned from that experience was the fragility of everything. Don’t take anything for granted. Anything can come and go in a moment. But I also worked with Lars Nilsson and Hervé Pierre Braillard, who were just the kindest people. This industry has a little bit of everything, but I loved that they led with kindness, even when they were under so much pressure. As an intern, I was literally carrying ironing boards down the street and doing a sketch here or there. It was very much about doing whatever needed to be done.

After my internship, I had a brief stint of freelancing. Those were some long months. I remember coming home from one job and my roommates asking how my day was. I said, “Well, I was putting pigs on socks.” I knew I wouldn’t be going back. Freelancing is hard. It’s a grind, but you meet a lot of great people. I actually made some really good contacts during that time. I eventually met Deirdre [Quinn], Lafayette 148’s founder. She met with me on a Saturday, which I thought was incredible. I was really just looking for advice. I wasn’t looking for a job, and I didn’t even know much about the brand. It was only five years old. She was so kind, full of knowledge, and passionate. After I spent a year freelancing and meeting people who seemed so over the industry, her enthusiasm reminded me why I wanted to do this in the first place. She offered me a part-time freelance position, and the rest is history.

In the beginning, security was really important to me. The idea of losing a job and having to pay rent was scary, so that was definitely part of it initially. But really, it was the growth. Within a couple of years, they were sending me to the factory. It was a small, tight-knit company, so I was able to wear a lot of different hats. I had a mentor named Barbara Gast who was traveling back and forth from Italy, and I was learning so much from her. I’d compare notes with friends in the industry and realize how much hands-on experience I was getting. I understood the value of that and really loved being so close to the product. It never got boring. And whenever things did get slightly boring, I’d ask, “Okay, what’s next?” And there was always something. It’s such an entrepreneurial place that you can almost create your next opportunity. That’s what made it so exciting.

I think if you asked Deirdre, she’d have a different answer because she has her own experience of building the company. For me, it’s about having started at a company that was really a factory and being part of the journey of building its identity and what it stands for. I was the kid running up and down the factory floors collecting samples. That hustle and bustle was so innate to who the brand was. To me, it was really exciting to build more of a brand story around that. Thirty years later, we’re still celebrating those roots and making sure we haven’t strayed too far from them, while continuing to evolve. Being part of that journey has been really exciting.

The constant has always been this idea of an accomplished woman. She’s always been at the forefront of who we’re designing for. At the time, it was the career woman. But now, what does that even mean anymore? What does that look like? There are so many different versions of that woman and so many different ways people dress. At the heart of it, she’s a woman who knows what she wants. She’s busy and has a really full life, whether she’s starting her career or ending it. They can all find something in the clothes.

For us, it was about choosing people who inspire us. Number one, they had to be New York women. That was the base. We wanted women who make us want to be better ourselves. From someone like Deborah Berke, the architect, to women who have built incredible careers in other fields, it’s important to shine a light on them. I think back to when I was a kid and how much you need that kind of inspiration. Even at a certain stage in your career, when you’re wondering what the point is, it’s nice to have people who inspire you. These are women who have really built something for themselves, and I think that’s worth celebrating.

Sophie de Rakoff said something during the project that I really liked, and I’m going to steal it: “Dressing with intention.” When you know yourself, you know what works on you. It’s no longer about dressing to impress. There’s a confidence in knowing what works for you and making it work. We’re all so busy. Who has time to overthink getting dressed? You know what works, and you build a system around that. You’re able to create a wardrobe that really works for you. Everybody has a different definition of a uniform, and that was the whole point of the project.

When I first started in the industry, I was a total hippie. I was making my own clothes, and they were terrible. Absolutely falling apart. It was what it was. I think part of the change comes from not having as much time as you did when you were younger. But it’s also about simplicity and comfort. I know that if I’m going to be on the floor pinning something but also have to give a presentation, there are certain pieces that work for both. I can be comfortable and still feel appropriately dressed. I’ve found a handful of things that work for me, and I don’t have to think too much about them anymore. A crisp, oversize white cotton button-down is half my closet. I also love a soft skirt and a big chunky sweater. Those are the pieces I always go back to and interchange depending on the day. I even wear sweaters in the summer. It’s cold in the Navy Yard!

Our pants fit incredibly well. The moment somebody gets into our pants, they’ll love us forever. Then it’s the jacket and the white shirt. Those three things are our gateway pieces, and everything else follows. You need a good blazer and a good leather piece, too. Once you find those foundational pieces that really work for you, everything else becomes easier.

I really want to see more women in our clothes. It’s not just about growing the business. It makes me happy when I see people put on our clothes and feel really good. We work so hard to make sure things fit the way a woman wants them to fit. I just want more people to enjoy that.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6917. Michelle Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Jill Biden Come Together at Gloria Steinem’s Joyous Celebration of Life

The former first ladies coordinated in elegant, high-fashion ensembles to honor the feminist activist

Gloria Steinem’s life, work, and legacy were celebrated this week, as many gathered at a memorial service for the feminist activist in New York City.

The celebration of life took place at the Park Avenue Armory and came two months after Steinem’s passing at age 92.

Among those who came together to pay their respects were former United States first ladies Michelle Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Jill Biden—as well as Chelsea Clinton, Diane von Furstenberg, Meg Ryan, Lucy Liu, Emma Watson, Marisa Tomei, and Mariska Hargitay. In total, there were about 1,000 invited guests, all who were encouraged to donate to Gloria’s Foundation, which aims to preserve Steinem’s Upper East Side brownstone on East 73rd Street as a permanent archive and center for feminist organizing.

Rather than a somber service, the memorial was a joyful, music-filled celebration titled “It’s Steinemite!” Cynthia Erivo sang John Lennon’s “Imagine,” Cyndi Lauper performed “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” and Kathy Sledge of Sister Sledge closed the event with “We Are Family,” joined by Lauper and Gloria’s Choir.

For the evening, attendees coordinated in all-black ensembles—but it certainly wasn’t your average funeral attire. Clinton wore an elegant pantsuit—one of her favored looks. Obama was so chic and cool in a cropped blazer and a pleated skirt with a silky sash and golden accents. And Biden went for a fun, high-fashion ensemble that included Schiaparelli’s black Corsini suit jacket with asymmetric gold buttons.

If she could’ve looked into that crowd of incredible women, Steinem would’ve been endlessly proud.

#6912. A Kitchen in Bloom: How Tiffany Howell and Miele Seductively Reimagine the Heart of the Home

Eschewing conventional design for an immersive, romantic kitchen, this wildly glamorous space proves that high-tech convenience can foster intimacy, slowness, and the art of living well.

When Tiffany Howell of Night Palm Interiors designs a home, her extraordinary vision transcends conventional norms, veering into an ethereal realm—an approach she calls “the poetry of place.” In Howell’s mind film, fashion, and music are as essential as decorative art, and, when designing a home, she uses all these inspirations to create theatrical spaces that ignite all the senses— layering texture, sound, scent, light, and form to evoke deep emotion. When executed with this level of intention, a room becomes an environment you don't merely look at but fundamentally feel.

When Miele asked Howell to create a dream kitchen for an installation at Art Basel, she seized the opportunity to reimagine what a kitchen can be. Set against the vibrant creative energy of Miami's premier art fair, the commission gave her a blank canvas to challenge utilitarian conventions and treat the culinary space as an ambitious work of living art. “I wanted an elevated sexiness, a beautiful, sensory experience,” she says. “I created the space with characters in mind that I’d invite to a dinner party in this kitchen.” After all, the kitchen is a home’s heartbeat, an interactive space with multiple purposes.

“I do think the kitchen is really one of the most tender rooms in the house,” Howell says. She leaned into that romance by installing black cabinetry with blossoming branches and birds in iridescent greens and pinks. The cabinets are an homage to her love of 1920s chinoiserie furniture and fashion, seen through a very glamourous, Los Angeles lens. That California focus also meant bringing the outdoors in. The grand conservatory space harnesses diffused, natural light with the promise of the scent of intoxicating jasmine wafting into the room. Howell’s ideal playlist sets the tone with jazz greats, and ambient synth-pop.

“I wanted to create a kitchen that’s a completely sensory experience,” Howell explains. “The sound of a crackling warm fireplace, the aroma of a meal cooked for loved ones, or of making coffee in the morning.” For Howell, these aren't incidental details; they are the sensory architecture that turns raw space into lived emotion. In Howell’s view, this kitchen is “also a place where you can take a nap, read a book, or write in your journal. Every moment in this room can become a ritualistic experience of living well.”

When it came to the practical needs of a kitchen, Howell used Miele as a muse, an invitation to eschew the pale minimalism so common in luxury kitchens. “The appliances are so elegant, they kind of act as the jewelry of the room,” she says. “And their functionality and ease of operation give you back time to live better, relax with a drink, hang out with family and friends, and create the stories that make up a life.”

Consider the Miele Built-In Coffee System and wine cooler in matching dark finishes which are nearly camouflaged so the technology reads more as furniture than appliance. That tension between heirloom design and high-tech styling becomes a unified part of a lived-in, well collected home. Accent pieces including a vintage Fortuny pendant lamp over the kitchen island, and upholstered chairs in the conservatory with detailing reminiscent of antique lingerie, create a moody environment well suited to Miele's black-finished lines that resemble rich obsidian.

The 36” Full Surface Induction Cooktop features a frameless, flush design that disappears into a dark-veined countertop. Transforming the entire glass surface into one expansive cooking area, it fits up to six pots or pans at once and with Intelligent Pan Recognition and SmartSelect White controls seamlessly transfer power settings wherever pans are moved. On the same wall is the 30” Handleless Combi-Steam Oven XXL, with DualSteam technology that emanates ASMR sounds of steam cooking, and a black glass façade that resembles a framed panel or window. From the cool, flush glide of the induction cooktop to the whisper-quiet hum of precision steam, the technology engages the senses rather than interrupting them, turning modern convenience into an intuitive, tactile ritual. Rather than breaking up the wall with a stack of conspicuous appliances, these seamless integrations keep the architecture artful. And for added convenience, Miele’s elegant touch controls are enhanced with WIFI connectivity for an easier user experience.

Howell’s concealment of technology is exhibited in her use of the 42” French Door Refrigerator with its elongated custom handles and a dark lacquered paneled front that echoes the floral chinoiserie motifs—an unconventional solution that turns a mundane appliance into a piece of decorative art. And once the refrigerator doors are open, the Brilliant Light Pro illumination makes it easy to survey the food inside the large capacity interior.

“How do you nurture yourself and others in the kitchen?” Howell asks. Her answer: a design that creates a restorative space evoking intimacy and slowness, where technology can encourage a lightness and give us back more time. By composing every sight, surface, scent, and sound into a single harmonious narrative, Howell proves that a kitchen shouldn't just be an aesthetic statement—it should be something you feel in your bones. “What excites me is building a new world with more possibilities,” Howell says. “I don’t think I could design any other way.”

#6909. All About Brittany Snow’s Fiancé, Hunter Moreno

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In October 2024, The Hunting Wives actress Brittany Snow was seen with a mystery man in New York City. He was identified as cinematographer Hunter Moreno, and the pair looked very cozy, sharing a kiss while walking Snow’s dog. The actress was wearing a Yankees cap, a long black coat, wide-leg pants, and a pair of sunglasses for the outing. Moreno was in a baseball cap, jeans, and a big white hoodie.

A year earlier, Snow divorced ex-husband Tyler Stanaland, known for his role on Selling the OC, a spinoff of the popular Netflix reality show, Selling Sunset.

The former couple announced their split in September 2022 in a joint statement on Instagram that is now deleted, saying, “This decision was made with love and mutual respect for one another. We have realized we need to take some time and make sure we are each living our most fulfilling and authentic lives. We started this journey as best friends and our relationship will continue to be a priority not only for us but for our dog Charlie.”

Fast-forward to November 2025: reports surfaced that Snow and Moreno had gotten engaged. Snow has since posted tributes to him on Instagram, though she rarely discusses their relationship status herself. A year later, she finally confirmed their engagement.

Here’s what there is to know about Moreno and his relationship with Snow so far.

Moreno is a creative director, cinematographer, and photographer who has worked with celebrities like Selena Gomez, Cara Delevingne, Reneé Rapp, Machine Gun Kelly, Miley Cyrus, and brands like Vogue, Inkd Magazine, and Madewell. He started his career in Los Angeles, filming YouTube videos for growing influencers.

He seems to have been working on directing more music videos in 2024 and was nominated for a directing award at the People’s Choice Country Awards.

He also briefly dated Tana Mongeau in 2017.

Moreno is the co-founder and creative director of Make Sure Your Friends Are OK, or MSYFAO. The organization sells merchandise and then donates a portion of the profits to mental health charities. In an episode of Recovering From Reality with Alexis Haines, he says he was inspired by his own struggles with mental health issues.

Mental health is an important issue to Snow as well; she co-wrote a book titled September Letters about issues around mental well-being, partnering with the Mental Health Coalition.

In January 2025, Snow tagged Moreno in a series of photos taken of her for a Netflix press event, crediting him for photographing her. She wrote, “I was asked to hang out a little bit with my friends at @nightagentnetflix. I got to be an agent and run around the streets of Bangkok. Weirdly, I did not wear this dress. 🤍* press for season 2 *”

As of July 2025, the two still follow each other on Instagram, and Moreno has liked almost all her recent Instagrams. She also regularly likes his posts.

Yes. On March 28, 2026, Snow quietly tucked a photo of herself with Moreno into an Instagram carousel:

She shared a birthday tribute to him on Oct. 20, 2026. “Happy birthday to my favorite person on the planet,” she wrote. “I must have done something right to deserve someone like you. Everyone who knows you, knows you are sunshine in human form. This was the first picture we ever took together (we didn’t know it was being taken) and I’ve never stopped hugging you & laughing with you since. It’s my favorite place to be. I love u @huntermoreno.”

During her November 2026 appearance on Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard, Snow touched on her relationship with Moreno when discussing why she is thankful for her divorce from Tyler Stanaland. “I am so grateful that I went through that because the person that I am and the partner I’m with now, it’s just so different,” she said. “I can’t believe I’m grateful for my divorce. I was 37 and I was living in an Airbnb, just staring at my dog being like, ‘I don’t know what’s going to happen. It’s just you and me, kiddo, and we’re going to try to rebuild this.’”

“And I really appreciated so many women, friends of mine that were like, ‘That happened to me,’” she added. “And, you know, I would go on Reddit and look up stories from women going through things in their later 30s and finding people later in life. We have to make it what we make of it.”

On Nov. 10, 2025, a video surfaced on social media of Snow and Claire Danes talking on the red carpet of The Beast in Me’s premiere. At one point, Danes smiled and asked Snow, “You’re engaged? When did that happen?”

One day later, TMZ reported that Moreno did indeed pop the question, though Snow has not discussed their status herself.

A year later, on Nov. 19, 2026, Snow finally confirmed the news on The Drew Barrymore Show. When Barrymore asked her about the news, Snow responded, per People, “You know what? For the first time, I’m gonna tell you, I’m gonna tell you. Yes, we’re engaged, yeah,” Snow said. “I haven’t said it before. It’s okay. It’s not that big of a secret. I mean, like, who cares?”

#6907. Has Zegna Cracked the Code to Modern Tailoring?

With its latest jacket, the Falcon, the brand brings some sporty utility to its collection of mix-and-matchable clothing. Artistic director Alessandro Sartori explains how it’s all part of a bigger project to help men dress their best.

Pay attention to the world of menswear long enough, and you’ll notice that certain quandaries come up time and again. A favorite among traditionalists and avant-garde types alike is the fate of the suit. It’s been incorrectly declared dead enough times that the handwringing over its demise has largely shifted to questions of its evolving role in the modern guy’s wardrobe: Who wears a suit, and when, and why?

According to Alessandro Sartori, the artistic director of Zegna for a little more than a decade now, there’s another question we should all be asking ourselves: What exactly is a suit these days?

“Everything we do here is grounded in tailoring techniques and in tailoring fabrics,” Sartori tells me over Zoom from his home in Milan. “But I'm a big believer that a suit doesn't necessarily have to be a combination of the classic top and the classic bottom in the same fabric and color.” It can be comprised of those things, he stresses. But the “modern suit,” as he calls it, can also be an intentional pairing of a different kind of top—a chore coat, an overshirt—with a trouser with a different fabrication. The materials and colors should feel complementary and cohesive but needn’t be perfectly matched.

“This is not only a way to give a new life to suiting,” he explains, “but to dress men differently—and, at the same time, keep the quality, the craft, and the beautiful fit that a tailored piece has.”

The idea is to adapt classic techniques to the realities of getting dressed today. “Many fashion brands offer a nice quality, but is not the handmade quality that we do,” Sartori says. “And there are a lot of brands that are offering beautiful, beautiful quality, but they are quite classic.” Since he started in 2016, Sartori’s overarching project has been to populate the gulf between those two modes of production, making clothes that feel contemporary but are rooted in the top-tier fabrics and handwork that helped Zegna become the powerhouse of Italian fashion that it is today.

The latest addition to Sartori’s lineup is a new jacket, the Falcon. It pays homage to the sort of utilitarian jackets Zegna founder Ermenegildo Zegna might have worn while walking the grounds of what is now the Oasi Zegna nature reserve in northern Italy, at the base of the Biellese Alps. (According to company lore, Ermenegildo imagined those walks as being accompanied by the flight of a falcon.)

Sartori acknowledges that the use case, in 2026, might be a little different. “I don't think that people are necessarily using the jacket walking up in the mountains,” he says. The Falcon is more about embracing a “sporty-chic attitude,” whether you’re stomping around the country or the city, and working within the modular framework that the designer has created at Zegna. You can mix and match it with other pieces—both old and new—from the brand, and you can wear it as part of a “modern suit” or on its own.

The new design is cut from Zegna’s Oasi Cashmere for lightweight warmth, and Sartori calls it “a great addition to our vocabulary.” Buttoned patch pockets give you somewhere to stash your stuff, a bowling collar can be flipped up to shield against stiff winds, and an internal drawstring can be cinched at the midsection for a little extra protection against the cold. Ultimately, it’s a familiar-looking piece. But it’s exceptional in its construction and materials and its design—a streamlined take on the hunting jackets of yore—is as considered as how it’s made.

“Long-lasting life is a key factor for what we're doing, and I don't mean only quality-wise,” Sartori says. “I also mean design-wise.”

The designer, for his part, hopes that the Falcon—alongside other modern classics from the brand—will be the sort of thing that guys wear and reinterpret for years before passing it on to the next generation. And as the brand continues to grow and evolve alongside its customer base, one of his biggest aims is to ensure that each item he introduces remains relevant throughout its (ideally long) lifespan.

“It’s like writing a book, and every season I add a chapter,” he says. “Because the story is going on, is moving with our clients, our community of people, our brand, our family. So many layers are … I don’t want to say ready, but cooking. I see a bright future for the brand, following this principle of walking with our customers and building an indelible aesthetic. I like this approach.”

He was also previously part of another group, called the Regrettes. In 2022, Lilly was invited to play on Cyrus’s TV special, Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party.

Throughout their years-long relationship, the two have preferred to keep their romance largely out of the spotlight. But Cyrus offered a rare glimpse into their life together during her interview for the Harper’s Bazaar’s December 2024/January 2025 cover story. “He’s very similar to me,” she said. “We just don’t take life too seriously.”

Throughout their time together, they’ve also collaborated numerous times in the studio, with Morando serving as a producer and songwriter on Cyrus’s Something Beautiful and Bass Persuades records. In her interview with Bazaar, Cyrus revealed that music was actually how she and Morando first got to know each other. “I’ve always worked with the people that I love,” Cyrus said. “And Maxx just inspires me so much.”

Now, the pair are engaged and reported to be getting married this weekend with an intimate ceremony in Southern California. However, other details are being kept under wraps—for now.

If you’re wondering what else there is to know about Cyrus and Morando’s low-key romance, then look no further. Below, we’ve tracked the couple’s entire relationship from start to finish.

For Cyrus, it was love at first sight, but for Morando, he already had an idea of who he was meeting long before the date even happened.

“We got put on a blind date,” Cyrus reveals in an interview with British Vogue years after the fact, in May 2023. “Well, it was blind for me and not really for him. I thought, ‘The worst that can happen is I leave.’ ”

When he calls mid-interview, her phone starts playing “Tyrone” by Erykah Badu. “I call that ‘boyfriend sexy ringtone,’ ” she says, smiling.

In an interview with Vogue, Cyrus discusses the outfits that she wore for her sets at Summerfest in Milwaukee and Atlanta’s Music Midtown festival. Turns out, one of the pieces—a faux-leather set crafted by Shane Kastl—includes cartoon monsters sketched by Morando.

During the interview, Cyrus comments on the custom design, saying, “This look is a one-of-a-kind collaboration between two of my favorite emerging artists, Maxx Morando and Shane Kastl. Shane used existing pieces I’ve collected over time and customized Maxx’s cartoon characters [within] his construction. Their collaboration is the perfect example of sustainability becoming the next fashion phase, and it proves that anything can be reinvented, which resonates with me deeply.”

The pair spark dating rumors when they make their first public appearance at the Gucci Love Parade fashion show in November.

For the event, Cyrus wears a metallic blue fringe dress with a contrasting cream feather drop waist, which she pairs with strappy golden sandals. Meanwhile, Morando sports a burgundy suit over a G-logo top, with white sneakers featuring the signature Gucci red and green stripes.

Shortly after the event, Cyrus shares a slideshow where the third photo sees her and Morando posing together on the red carpet. In her caption, the singer writes, “LOVE PARADE ❤️💕 @gucci @alessandro_michele.”

A fan captures a sweet video of Morando supporting Cyrus backstage for her NBC holiday special, Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party. In the clip, the two can be seen smiling and dancing together.

Days later, paparazzi snap photos of the two enjoying a vacation together in Miami, where the special was filmed.

Cyrus and Morando make a rare joint appearance together for Versace’s Fall/Winter 2023 fashion show in West Hollywood.

Later in the day, the two attend the launch party for Cyrus’s eighth studio album, Endless Summer Vacation, in Beverly Hills. Paparazzi photos—which you can see here—show Cyrus dressed to the nines in a sparkly black one-shoulder minidress and a vibrant green fur jacket. Morando looks equally stylish in a navy-blue velvet suit.

A source tells People where Cyrus’s head is at amid her relationship with Morando.

“She’s the healthiest and happiest she’s been in a long time,” the source says, then goes on to describe how Cyrus has healed following her 2020 divorce from Liam Hemsworth: “Everyone was blaming her for the divorce and calling her this wild child, but that wasn’t fair. Their relationship and marriage was toxic, and she was heartbroken.”

A second insider tells the outlet that Morando is a “cool guy.”

“He has no interest in being a huge celebrity; he’s very low-key. Miley loves these qualities,” the source explains. “Miley can be herself. They are supportive of each other’s careers. Miley is enjoying life and things are great.”

Morando supports Cyrus at the 66th-annual Grammy Awards ceremony, where the singer wins her first-ever golden gramophone.

During the ceremony, the couple is joined by Cyrus’s family members, mom Tish Cyrus and sister Brandi Cyrus.

A source for People opens up about Cyrus and Morando’s joyful home life together.

“She is very happy with him,” the insider claims. “Miley has changed a lot in the past couple of years. She seems more calm and harmonious. Everyone loves Maxx. He’s a great guy. She is very happy with him. He’s private and doesn’t like being in the press. It’s been good for her.”

In a new Dolce & Gabbana campaign video, Cyrus poses in a sultry all-black look and shares the song “Imitate,” a track from Morando’s band, Liily.

Cyrus offers rare details on her love story with Morando in an interview for Bazaar’s December 2024/January 2025 cover story.

“He’s very similar to me. We just don’t take life too seriously,” she says.

While the two have a small age gap—Cyrus is six years Morando’s senior—she reflects on how their different upbringings have made them approach life differently.

“He looks at life really differently than I do,” she explains. “He grew up with a laptop. I had a desktop computer that I shared with my brothers and sisters. … Honestly, he’s raised our dog off Reddit. I’m like, Are you sure we’re supposed to be doing this? And he’s like, On Reddit it says blah, blah, blah.”

She also opens up about working with Morando on musical projects and how collaboration is her love language. “I worked with my dad forever. That’s how me and my ex-husband met each other. I’ve always worked with the people that I love,” Cyrus says. “And Maxx just inspires me so much.”

Morando and Cyrus are photographed behind-the-scenes at the 67th Grammy Awards, where Cyrus snags her third Grammy for her collaboration on Beyoncé’s “II Most Wanted.” The appearance marks a rare joint public outing by the couple, who match in all-black ensembles.

Morando wears his usual red-carpet uniform to stand by his partner at the 97th Academy Awards. Cyrus wears a black gown with a distressed bodice embellished with sequins, which she wears with a curly hairdo and bleached brows.

Cyrus and Morando walk the red carpet for the Hollywood premiere of Avatar: Fire and Ash, and there, the singer debuts a chunky gold ring with a large, square diamond at the center.

Hours later, People confirms the two are engaged.

The engaged pair wear cool all-black looks to the show and look so in love as they embrace at their star-studded table during the ceremony.

Cyrus is sleek in a moto-inspired fit from Celine, while Morando goes low-key in a black T-shirt and pants.

Following their engagement news, a source tells People that the couple wants a “smaller and meaningful” wedding rather than a “huge, traditional” event.

While it’s unclear when the Hannah Montana singer plans to wed her drummer fiancé, the source says Cyrus is enjoying this era and her engagement: “Miley really loves her life right now. Everything just feels like it’s falling into place for her.”

At the world premiere of the Hannah Montana 20th Anniversary Special in Los Angeles, Cyrus walks the red carpet alongside her fiancé.

For the occasion, the Disney Channel alum wears a plunging silver Rabanne dress layered over a bedazzled Hannah Montana tee, while her beau opts for a white tee and black jeans, which he pairs with black-and-white sneakers from Celine.

Cyrus is honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, thanks to her “lasting impact on the entertainment industry.” In reference to Cyrus’s work on Hannah Montana and more, Walk of Fame producer Ana Martinez notes: “Generations of young girls have grown up watching her evolve, finding inspiration in her journey and fearless creativity.”

At the ceremony, Cyrus is supported by members of her family like mom Tish and her older half-sister, Brandi. Meanwhile, Morando shows his support too, posing with Cyrus in front of the plaque.

Nearly a year after the pair reveal their engagement, TMZ reports that they will tie the knot with a secret ceremony in Southern California, scheduled to take place on the weekend of November 20.
